Use this as a self-audit. Anything you cannot tick, re-read the section in parentheses. Tick honestly — the goal is to find the three gaps worth spending the next evening on, not to collect 100 ticks.

## A. Patterns — can I explain, not just recognise?

- [ ] I can state intent, participants, and consequences for any GoF pattern I name. (§11.1.1)
- [ ] I can argue **against** Singleton on five named grounds, and name the one defensible use. (§11.1.2)
- [ ] I can say Factory Method vs Abstract Factory in one sentence each, with the axis-count rule. (§11.1.3)
- [ ] I can write a Builder with real validation, and explain when an options object is better. (§11.1.4)
- [ ] I can distinguish Adapter (one), Facade (many), Bridge (two axes) without hesitating. (§11.1.5)
- [ ] I can explain decorator ordering, the forwarding tax, and the `Proxy` thenable trap. (§11.1.6, §11.1.7)
- [ ] I can enumerate the six design decisions in an event emitter and defend each. (§11.1.8)
- [ ] I know the undo-stack invariant and why compensation is not rollback. (§11.1.9, §11.1.16)
- [ ] I can distinguish Strategy from State without relying on a mnemonic. (§11.1.10, §11.1.11)
- [ ] I can name Template Method's hook-explosion failure and its composition replacement. (§11.1.12)
- [ ] I can say what Repository/UoW/Data Mapper each solve, and where Active Record is fine. (§11.1.13)
- [ ] I can argue manual DI over a container, and name the two DI lifetimes that matter. (§11.1.14)
- [ ] I can name the resilience family and give the one-line rule for each. (§11.1.15)
- [ ] I can state what event-driven architecture **does not** decouple. (§11.1.17)
- [ ] I can name at least six pattern anti-patterns with their fixes. (§11.1.18)

## B. OOP, SOLID, clean code

- [ ] I can give a before/after that makes an invalid state unrepresentable. (§11.2.1)
- [ ] I can show composition replacing a combinatorial hierarchy, **and** an inheritance case I would keep. (§11.2.2)
- [ ] I can write the before/after for all five SOLID principles. (§11.2.3)
- [ ] I can apply DRY to *knowledge* rather than text, and name the four DRY failure modes. (§11.2.4)
- [ ] I can define the stopping rule for abstraction ("two implementations, a domain name, or a volatile dependency"). (§11.2.4)
- [ ] I can name my naming rules, especially units and the four-name-per-concept rule. (§11.2.5)
- [ ] I can fix four smells with the named refactoring for each. (§11.2.6)
- [ ] I can draw hexagonal ports and adapters and name six boundary leaks. (§11.2.7)
- [ ] I can name the five DDD building blocks and the aggregate rules. (§11.2.8)
- [ ] I can defend an anemic model for a *named* case, not in general. (§11.2.9)
- [ ] I can describe the legacy workflow: characterisation test → seam → small refactor → strangler. (§11.2.10)

## C. Architectural styles

- [ ] I can argue the monolith is the default, with four reasons microservices do not fix. (§11.3.1)
- [ ] I know four ways to enforce module boundaries, and that architecture tests are the one that works. (§11.3.2)
- [ ] I can name the seven leaks of layered architecture. (§11.3.3)
- [ ] I can state microservices' three real gains and ten costs. (§11.3.4)
- [ ] I can complete the six-criterion decision card and say what the score means. (§11.3.5)
- [ ] I can explain dual-write and implement an outbox relay with a claim. (§11.3.6)
- [ ] I know the three CQRS levels and the read-your-writes options. (§11.3.7)
- [ ] I can give the honest event-sourcing trade-off, including upcasters and erasure. (§11.3.8)
- [ ] I can name the four serverless constraints and the function-per-request trap. (§11.3.9)
- [ ] I can define a BFF and name its three jobs and three non-jobs. (§11.3.10)
- [ ] I know what a mesh buys, what it costs, and that the control plane must be out of the data path. (§11.3.11)
- [ ] I can talk about CRDTs and quorum replication without overclaiming. (§11.3.12)
- [ ] I can walk the six questions and defend a decision without saying "it depends". (§11.3.13)

## D. Low-level design — can I build these cold?

- [ ] Parking lot: atomic allocation, two strategies, indexed queries, fee rounding. (§11.4.1)
- [ ] LRU cache: O(1) both ways, `peek` semantics, TTL, single-flight, LFU variant. (§11.4.2)
- [ ] Rate limiter: three algorithms, Redis atomicity, fail-open/closed, idle eviction. (§11.4.3)
- [ ] Elevator: state machine with a transition table, reversal rules, dispatch strategies. (§11.4.4)
- [ ] Splitwise: integer money, Σ=0 invariant, greedy simplification, deletion reversal. (§11.4.5)
- [ ] Tic-tac-toe: immutability, undo, minimax + alpha-beta, a property test. (§11.4.6)
- [ ] Notification service: preferences precedence, cascade, dedupe key, retries, DLQ. (§11.4.7)
- [ ] Logger: early exit, bounded buffer, single-flight drain, redaction, dedupe. (§11.4.8)
- [ ] Library system: title vs copy, reservation hold window, renewal rules, fine policy. (§11.4.9)
- [ ] I have implemented and **run** at least six of the ten from-scratch problems. (§11.4 Problems)

## E. Interview performance

- [ ] I can produce a class diagram for all nine case studies in under three minutes each.
- [ ] I can state the state and invariants for all nine without looking.
- [ ] For each case study I can name the "tricky part" and the concurrency answer in one sentence.
- [ ] I can give an extension point for every case study that a real product would need.
- [ ] I have critiqued all twelve review scenarios and ranked defects by severity.
- [ ] I can answer any of the 40 Q&A questions in under 90 seconds with the trade-off included.
- [ ] I can do all 60 rapid-fire items in 15 seconds each.

## F. Final self-check — the three questions that decide the interview

- [ ] **Can I name a requirement behind every abstraction I create?** If not, I am guessing and should revert.
- [ ] **Can I name the trade-off I paid for each design decision?** If not, it was not a decision.
- [ ] **Can I state what I deliberately did NOT do, and why?** This is the strongest signal of senior judgement.

---

## Where to spend the remaining evening

Rank your gaps by *frequency × severity* and fix at most three:

1. **Any unchecked item in section A or B** — the fundamentals get asked in almost every system-design round, including frontend and data roles. Fix these first.
2. **Any unchecked item in section C** — the decision framework (C13) is the single most-likely artifact in a senior interview. If you cannot complete the decision card, practise that.
3. **Any unchecked item in D or E** — pick the case studies you cannot draw from memory and rehearse them out loud, then implement the two you have never coded.

Do not spend the evening re-reading. Spend it **producing**: draw the diagrams, write the code, say the answers out loud. Design skill is procedural, not declarative — you improve it by running the procedure under time pressure, not by re-reading the manual.

topics.title: What a pattern is, and the three things every pattern has
topics.description: A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem. It is not a library, not a language feature, and — critically — not code you copy. It is *vocabulary plus structure plus a documented cost*. When a reviewer says "that's a Strategy here," they are not commenting on your code style; they are naming a known trade-off so the next person does not have to rediscover it.
keyConcepts: Difficulty

Intent — what problem it solves, stated in one sentence that does not mention the solution's mechanics. "Allow a client to add new behaviour without changing a class that already uses it." Note the absence of the word "Strategy." A pattern's intent should survive a total rewrite of its implementation.

topics.title: Singleton and why it is almost always the wrong answer
topics.description: Singleton restricts a class to exactly one instance and provides a global point of access to it.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Why it is almost always the wrong answer

It is a hidden dependency. AppConfig.getInstance() appears in the middle of a function whose signature promises nothing about configuration. The dependency is invisible to the reader, to the type system, and to every tool that traces calls. Compare new BillingService(config) — the dependency is in the signature, greppable, and free to vary.

It is untestable. You cannot pass a different instance to the code under test. Tests mutate global state, so they cannot run in parallel and they leak state between cases. This is why singleton code produces the notorious beforeEach { Config.reset() } in every spec file that touches it.

It owns its own lifecycle. Singletons initialise lazily, forever, on first use. In a server, that means initialisation can happen on the hot path of the first request under a lock; in a test, it means state survives between tests. Both are the container's job, not the class's.

It destroys testability of module boundaries. It creates a *global mutable variable*, which means any two parts of the program can interfere. Under concurrency you now need to reason about which of your 40 threads might be reading config mid-reassignment.

It is not actually one instance, it is one instance per realm. In Node with ESM/CJS interop you get two; in a browser with iframes you get several; in a cluster you get one *per worker*. So Singleton usually fails to deliver even the thing it promises while still delivering the costs.
Real code: the three replacements, in order of preference
A genuinely defensible Singleton
The object is stateless or immutable (a pure function table, a lookup table of currency codes, a regex cache). Then "singleton" degenerates to "module constant" and there is no coupling problem.

The object is a process-level resource with expensive acquisition — a thread pool, a native library handle, an open TLS context. Here the real concerns are thread-safe lazy init and guaranteed release. Prefer an explicit acquire()/release() or a container-managed singleton over a class-managed one.
The language/runtime gives you process-wide state anyway — a global event loop, a standard output stream, an interpreter registry — and re-implementing it adds nothing.

topics.description: Factory Method, Abstract Factory, and the concrete vs abstract distinction within Design Patterns.
keyConcepts: Difficulty

Factory Method defines an interface for *creating one kind of object* (a single product) and defers the concrete class to subclasses. The method that builds the thing lives in the same class hierarchy as the thing being built, or in a dedicated creator that subclasses override.

Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating a *family of related objects* without specifying their concrete classes. The caller gets a "kit" whose parts are guaranteed to be mutually compatible.
The concrete vs abstract distinction you must be able to state
When abstract factory is the right answer (and it is a narrow answer)
Factory Method has one abstract creation method per creator class.
Abstract Factory has several abstract creation methods per factory, and returns products of *several* types.
Abstract Factory is usually composed *with* a strategy or registry to select the family.
Real code: the version you will actually write in a service
Factory Method: when a base class owns an algorithm with one variable step and you want subclasses to vary only that step. Also when you need to *test* the algorithm with a stub product.
Abstract Factory: when product families must be mutually consistent and the number of families is small.

The problem, stated precisely
Builder with mandatory fields done properly

topics.title: Adapter, Facade, and Bridge
topics.description: Adapter, Facade, and Bridge within Design Patterns.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Adapter
Facade
Bridge
Interviewer recognition test

Adapter: always, whenever a third-party or legacy interface meets your interface. Cost is near zero and the payoff (one place to fix vendor breakage) is enormous. This is the highest value-to-cost ratio pattern in the entire catalog.
Facade: when a caller needs a *workflow*, not a single operation. Do not use it to hide a single subsystem's API — a facade with one subsystem is a pointless wrapper.

topics.title: Decorator vs Wrapper, and where JavaScript's own language features do this for free
topics.description: A Decorator attaches additional behaviour to an object by *wrapping it* while keeping the same interface. topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Difficulty:** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Definition.** A Proxy is a stand-in for another object that intercepts operations on it. In design-pattern terms it is the structural version of Decorator: instead of hand-forwarding each method, you intercept property access generically. JavaScript ships this as a language feature, so "the Proxy pattern" and "the JS `Proxy` API" are the same conversation.

**Mechanics: the 13 traps, and which ones matter.** `new Proxy(target, handler)` supports `get`, `set`, `has`, `deleteProperty`, `ownKeys`, `defineProperty`, `getPrototypeOf`, `setPrototypeOf`, `isExtensible`, `preventExtensions`, `apply`, `construct`, `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`. Five matter in practice:

```ts
const trace = <T extends object>(obj: T, label: string, log: Log): T =>
  new Proxy(obj, {
    get(t, p, r)      { const v = Reflect.get(t, p, t); log.trace(`${label}.${String(p)}`);
                         return typeof v === 'function' ? v.bind(t) : v; },
    set(t, p, v)      { log.trace(`${label}.set(${String(p)})`); return Reflect.set(t, p, v, t); },
    has(t, p)         { return Reflect.has(t, p); },
    deleteProperty(t, p) { log.trace(`${label}.delete(${String(p)})`); return Reflect.deleteProperty(t, p); },
    ownKeys(t)        { return Reflect.ownKeys(t); },
  });

// Invariants that bite: a non-configurable, non-writable own property MUST report the same value
// from get; ownKeys MUST include all non-configurable own keys of the target; a `get` that returns a
// different function each call breaks `===` comparisons on methods and can break `Object.keys`.
```

`Reflect.*` is not decoration: using `Reflect` instead of hand-writing the default behaviour is what makes the proxy forward correctly for accessors, receivers, and `this`-typed private fields. `Reflect.get(t, p, t)` with the *target* as receiver is required if the target has private class fields (`#x`), because private fields are brand-checked against the receiver.

**Real uses, in rough order of production value.**

1. **Boundary validation and normalisation.** A Proxy in front of parsed external input converts "trust the payload" into "validate the payload", without you writing a DTO per field.

```ts
// Deep freeze + validate + default-fill at the edge, one place, no per-field ceremony.
function hardened<T extends object>(raw: unknown, spec: FieldSpec): T {
  const out = structuredClone(raw);
  for (const [k, rule] of Object.entries(spec)) {
    const v = (out as Record<string, unknown>)[k];
    const coerced = rule.coerce(v);
    if (!coerced.ok) throw new InvalidField(k, coerced.reason);
    (out as Record<string, unknown>)[k] = coerced.value;
  }
  return deepFreeze(out) as T;
}
```

2. **Lazy initialisation / virtual fields.** A Proxy that materialises a field from a loader on first access removes the `if (!this.x) this.x = load()` pattern from constructors.

3. **Memoisation.** Intercept `get`, look up a WeakMap cache, compute on miss. Careful: the cache key must be the *receiver*, not the proxy, or you get infinite recursion. And you must not memoise anything with a side effect.

4. **Read-only views.** A Proxy that throws on `set`/`delete`/`defineProperty` makes immutability real rather than `readonly`-by-convention (`readonly` in TypeScript compiles away; `Object.freeze` is shallow).

5. **Deprecation shims and API migration.** Wrap a legacy module and log which old methods are still called — you get migration telemetry for free, and the shim disappears when the log goes quiet.

6. **ORM/SDK property-access translation** — a snake_case API exposed as camelCase.

7. **Tracing instrumentation** — the `logged` decorator from 11.1.6.

**When to use vs not.**

- **Use** when the interception is *generic* (applies to all properties) or *derived from data* (a spec-driven validator), or when the value is genuinely lazy and expensive.
- **Use** in dev/test code: a debug Proxy that logs unexpected property reads is a fantastic way to find which properties of a mock a test actually depends on.
- **Don't use** on hot paths: every property access becomes a trap with megamorphic dispatch; a Proxy-heavy inner loop can be several times slower than the plain version, and it defeats inline caches.
- **Don't use** when a plain function or a class does the job. `Proxy` is the most powerful and least readable tool in this file; reach for it when a data-driven rule makes hand-written code unmaintainable.
- **Don't use** for security. A Proxy is not a sandbox — `getPrototypeOf`, `getPrototypeOf` chains, `Symbol` access, and `Function.prototype.toString` all leak structure. Anything adversarial gets a real realm (`vm`, WASM, a subprocess).

**Trade-offs.** You gain: one place for a whole class of concerns, zero per-field code, composability. You pay: (a) readability — a reader sees `p.foo` and cannot know a trap runs; (b) debuggability — the stack shows the proxy, not the target; (c) invariants — you can throw `TypeError` from a proxy that violates an invariant, which is the worst class of bug; (d) performance on hot paths; (e) `typeof`, `instanceof`, and identity subtleties that surprise people (`p instanceof Foo` works; `p.constructor` returns your trapped value if you trap it wrong).

**Production considerations.**

- **Never** return a different value than the target for non-writable, non-configurable properties.
- `ownKeys` must be consistent with `getOwnPropertyDescriptor` results, or `Object.keys` throws "proxy trap result is inconsistent".
- If you trap `get` for functions, bind to the target (or `Reflect.get(t,p,t)`) or methods using private fields throw `TypeError: Cannot read private member`.
- Proxies around classes break `super` in some edge cases; prefer wrapping *instances*/plain objects than prototypes.
- A Proxy around a network client leaks the target if you forget `getPrototypeOf`; combine with an allowlist if the input is untrusted.
- Memory: a WeakMap-keyed cache keyed by the *proxy* (rather than the target) leaks nothing, because the WeakMap entry dies with the proxy — but it also never hits. Key by target and store the proxy.

**Common mistakes.**

1. Forgetting `Reflect` and losing accessor behaviour.
2. Catching everything in `get` and returning `undefined` for typos — silent `undefined is not a function` three layers away.
3. Using a Proxy as a validation boundary and calling it "security".
4. Proxying the request object in a hot express handler "for convenience".
5. Not remembering that `for...in` uses `ownKeys` + `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, and `JSON.stringify` uses `ownKeys` + `get` — a proxy that only traps `get` will serialise to `{}`.

**Interviewer probes.**
- *"What happens if your proxy `get` trap returns a function for every property?"* — `then` becomes a function, so the proxy becomes *thenable*, and `await proxy` hangs forever or resolves to the wrong thing. This is the classic Proxy footgun.
- *"How do you debug a Proxy?"* — `console.dir`/`util.inspect` custom hooks, plus logging inside the traps; the target is reachable via a closure if you keep it.
- *"Why not just use getters?"* — getters are per-class and cannot be data-driven across third-party objects; Proxy is the only interception point that works on objects you do not control.

- Memory: a WeakMap-keyed cache keyed by the *proxy* (rather than the target) leaks nothing, because the WeakMap entry dies with the proxy — but it also never hits. Key by target and store the proxy.

**Common mistakes.**

1. Forgetting `Reflect` and losing accessor behaviour.
2. Catching everything in `get` and returning `undefined` for typos — silent `undefined is not a function` three layers away.
3. Using a Proxy as a validation boundary and calling it "security".
4. Proxying the request object in a hot express handler "for convenience".
5. Not remembering that `for...in` uses `ownKeys` + `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, and `JSON.stringify` uses `ownKeys` + `get` — a proxy that only traps `get` will serialise to `{}`.

**Interviewer probes.**
- *"What happens if your proxy `get` trap returns a function for every property?"* — `then` becomes a function, so the proxy becomes *thenable*, and `await proxy` hangs forever or resolves to the wrong thing. This is the classic Proxy footgun.
- *"How do you debug a Proxy?"* — `console.dir`/`util.inspect` custom hooks, plus logging inside the traps; the target is reachable via a closure if you keep it.
- *"Why not just use getters?"* — getters are per-class and cannot be data-driven across third-party objects; Proxy is the only interception point that works on objects you do not control.

topics.title: Observer and the event emitter as its canonical implementation
topics.description: Observer defines a one-to-many dependency: when a Subject changes state, all registered Observers are notified automatically. The canonical implementation in every language is the event emitter / event bus.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
on returns an unsubscribe function. If it does not, you cannot remove a listener, and you leak the listener *and its captured scope* for the life of the process.

A Set, not an array. Duplicate subscriptions are a real bug class (a module re-imported in dev adds the listener twice; you get double-sent notifications in dev only, which is the worst possible place to find it).

Copy before iterating. A listener that unsubscribes during dispatch otherwise mutates the collection mid-loop: in JS that skips listeners; in other languages it throws ConcurrentModificationException. This is a genuine production incident (self-unsubscribing one-shot listeners).
Per-event keying. A single array means off is O(n) and emit must filter; a Map<event, Set> makes both cheap and makes "no listeners for this event" detectable.

Typed event map. Record<string, unknown> gives you a compile error when a payload shape changes and a typo error on the event name. This is the difference between an event bus as an asset and as a liability.

Error isolation. The version above lets a throwing listener abort the remaining listeners. That is a decision: decide it explicitly. The robust version catches per-listener, reports the error, and continues — because "one bad analytics listener stopped order confirmation" is a real bug.
Observer's two cousins and the distinction that matters
Observer: the Subject *knows* its Observers and typically calls them directly. Coupling is compile-time visible.

Reactive (RxJS): cold/hot semantics, backpressure via bufferSize, cancellation via AbortSignal, and switchMap/concatMap for concurrency control. If you have any rate-limited source, you want this, not a callback list.
Pub/Sub (11.1.17): publishers and subscribers never reference each other, usually across a broker.

Use: when the set of reactions to an event is *open* (will grow), when reactions are optional and independent (analytics, cache invalidation, email), when the number of subscribers varies per deployment, or when you genuinely want to break a compile-time dependency on a downstream consumer.

topics.title: Command and the undo stack
topics.description: Command encapsulates a request as an object. That object can carry parameters, be stored, be queued, be logged, and — the reason the pattern exists in most UI code — be *executed later or reversed*.
keyConcepts: Difficulty

Non-invertible commands. ResizeCanvas(w, h) cannot be inverted without storing the old size. So every invertible command must capture its prior state *at construction or execute time*, not try to reconstruct it at undo time.

Partial failure. MoveShape succeeded, RecolorShape failed. Now the stack top is RecolorShape, which never ran, but the state reflects a moved shape. You must decide: push only on success (above), or push before and mark as failed. The correct default is push only on success and record the failure separately.

Non-LIFO dependencies. Undoing AddB after AddA was undone breaks the invariant. This is why real editors store *commands in a document timeline* with an inverse stored at execution time, not a naive stack.

Server authority. Undo on the client that the server disagrees with is a data-integrity incident. Undo must be a *command sent to the authority* that returns an inverse, not a client-side state edit. This is the difference between undo in Figma and undo in a notepad.

Use: undo/redo; operation queues and job dispatch; operation logging and replay; throttled/serialised access to a mutable resource (each command captures its own parameters so no shared mutable state leaks); anything where you need to *defer* or *retry with identical parameters*.
Use for Command + Invoker + Receiver when you need a queue that serialises access — one worker, commands in order, no locking.
Don't use: for every method call. Wrapping add(a,b) in a AddCommand class with an execute() that calls calculator.add(a,b) adds a class and zero capability.
Don't use when the receiver must run immediately and return a value to the caller — that is a function.
Bounded stack. Never unbounded; a text editor holding a million commands is an OOM. Bound it and make the eviction policy visible ("earliest 100 commands are not undoable").
Redo stack is the mirror: on undo, push the command and any captured inverse onto the redo stack; on execute, clear the redo stack.
Coalescing. Repeated identical commands (typing) should collapse — replace the top of the stack if it has the same coalesceKey and is recent. This is what keeps memory bounded in real editors.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain difficulty and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Gain: deferred/queued execution, serialisability, undo, logging, uniform error handling and retry at the invoker level, and a uniform place to add authorisation/validation ("every command passes through the same guard").

topics.title: Strategy and the switch statement it replaces
topics.description: Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, encapsulates each in its own class, and makes them independently swappable via a common interface.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The problem
AFTER

Use: when a decision is *made at runtime from data* (config, DB column, request field, user segment), when the alternatives are genuinely different *algorithms* rather than variations of one, and when each alternative has enough behaviour to deserve its own test file.
Use: when you want the *decision to be testable in isolation* — the biggest practical win.
Don't use for a switch over an enum with 3–4 trivial branches, each one line. That is the "switch that is fine"; replacing it with 5 files and a registry is a net loss in readability.
Don't use when all branches share 95% of their body (the Strategy classes become 95% identical, or worse, they all delegate to a shared helper so you gained a layer and no clarity).
Don't use when the alternatives differ only in *data* — that is a table/config, not a strategy. { vip: 0.9, student: 0.85 } beats five classes.
Real code: the dependency-injected version that scales better
Selection must fail loudly. Unknown segment ⇒ explicit default or throw, never undefined.
Strategies hold state? Prefer stateless strategies held in a DI container as singletons; if a strategy must be stateful, construct it per request.
Persistence: the segment string in the database is a contract. Renaming 'vip' to 'vip-annual' without a migration will silently price orders with the default rule. Migrate the data.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain difficulty and when you would use it.
Explain the problem and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* open/closed, runtime swappable, per-strategy tests, no central place where the decision list can rot.

topics.title: State and the state machine connection
topics.description: State lets an object alter its behaviour when its internal state changes, by delegating to a strategy object per state. The object appears unchanged to the client but its *available operations* change.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The problem: the boolean explosion
AFTER
The State-vs-Strategy distinction, precisely (memorise this)
Three concrete benefits you must be able to argue

The legal graph becomes data. You can draw it, put it in a table, generate docs from it, and — critically — write a *reachability test*: enumerate all states and all operations and assert the transition table matches your spec. With a boolean representation this test is impossible to write.
The state name is available for free for metrics, error messages, and API responses. doc.status is this.state.name.
Adding a state does not require auditing every method — you add a class and register it in the transition map.

Use: when an object has (a) ≥3 states, (b) a transition graph with real constraints, (c) behaviour that differs by state, and (d) illegal combinations that must be impossible rather than merely forbidden.
Use for: order/invoice/subscription lifecycles, workflow engines, protocol state machines, game entity AI, UI wizard steps, job pipelines.
Don't use: two states (use a boolean and a guard), or states that differ only in data (use a field).
Don't use: when transitions must be *auditable for compliance* and the transitions happen inside framework callbacks — then persist an explicit transition log/event instead of relying on the object.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain difficulty and when you would use it.
Explain the state-vs-strategy distinction, precisely (memorise this) and when you would use it.
Explain three concrete benefits you must be able to argue and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* behaviour that cannot be called in the wrong state, self-documenting legal graph, no guard soup, per-state unit tests, free status name.

topics.title: Template Method and the inheritance trap
topics.description: Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and lets subclasses override specific steps. It is inheritance-based, and that is both its use and its fatal weakness.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The honest case for it
The inheritance trap, stated concretely

The hook explosion. When you need a job that skips validation but adds a transform, you either override validate to return a lie (return ok(rows) without validating), or you get an if in the base class (if (this.shouldValidate)), and now the template has a hole shaped exactly like your new requirement. After three such requirements the template is a switch with steps around it.

Every subclass sees every step. A subclass that only wants to override parsing is forced to implement persist, because the base declared it abstract. You have created coupling to steps it does not care about.

Testing requires subclassing. You cannot test the template without faking the steps, so your test file defines a TestImportJob extends ImportJob — and if the base class has any *concrete* step that touches the network or the DB, your test is broken or slow. Template Method is hostile to composition-based test doubles precisely because the seams are inheritance-based, not constructor-injection-based.
The hierarchy is permanent. Every new variation is a new subclass; the tree only grows. You cannot compose "a CSV fetcher with an S3 parser" because they are peers in the hierarchy, not layers.
Shadowing hazards. A subclass declaring a private method with the same name as a base method silently breaks polymorphism; super.method() calls get confusing.

Use (rarely): algorithm with ≥5 steps and a fixed order, where only 1–2 steps vary, and the number of subclasses will stay under ~3. Classic: JUnit lifecycle hooks, java.util.logging, JDBC Template, ORM lifecycle callbacks, HTTP request pipeline in a framework you control.
Use when you *are building the framework* and want to force an extension structure on your users — the framework author legitimately owns the skeleton.
Don't use in application code you own when there is more than one or two variable steps.
Don't use when you need runtime composition (choose behaviour from data).

interviewQuestions.text: Explain difficulty and when you would use it.
Explain the honest case for it and when you would use it.
Explain the inheritance trap, stated concretely and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* algorithm in one place, guaranteed step order, shared default steps, extension points that are enforced by the compiler.

topics.title: Repository, Unit of Work, and Data Mapper
topics.description: Repository, Unit of Work, and Data Mapper within Design Patterns.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Data Mapper
Repository
Unit of Work
The three tools that replace manual change tracking
Explicit marking (above): registerDirty(obj) — most control, most to forget.
Identity Map + dirty tracking via Object.freeze + a Proxy that records sets (from 11.1.7) — automatic, magic, hard to debug.
Session-attached objects (Hibernate Session, EF DbContext, Active Record) — you give up domain purity and gain automatic change tracking and lazy loading.
The Lazy Loading trap, which is where purity dies
Data Mapper: whenever the storage shape differs from the domain shape, or you want the domain model free of persistence concerns. This is the default choice in a serious codebase.

Repository: when you have multiple aggregates, want to fake them in tests, or want queries expressed in domain language. Do not build a generic BaseRepository<T, TId> that mirrors your ORM — that is a wrapper with no value.
Unit of Work: when a business operation touches several aggregates and must be atomic. If every operation touches exactly one row and the DB's own transaction handles it, a Unit of Work is overhead.

topics.title: Dependency Injection and IoC containers
topics.description: Dependency Injection (DI) is supplying a class's collaborators from outside rather than constructing them inside. Inversion of Control (IoC) is the general principle; a container is one mechanism for achieving it. Critical distinction: DI does not require a container.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Why DI
Fakes instead of mocks. A constructor parameter typed as an interface can be replaced with an in-memory implementation. A new inside a method cannot.

Determinism. Inject Clock, IdGenerator, Random, and your tests stop being flaky. A codebase that injects Clock has no jest.useFakeTimers; a codebase that calls Date.now() deep in a domain service has flaky tests forever.
Scope control. Whether something is a singleton, per-request, or per-test becomes a decision in the composition root rather than an accident of static.
Decoupling for change. Swapping a payment provider touches the composition root and the adapter, not the service.
The five kinds of injection, and which to use
An IoC container
Registration: bind(Foo).to(PostgresFoo), bind(Token).to(Impl).singleton(), bind(Foo).toFactory(...).
Resolution: the container walks the graph, resolving each constructor parameter by type token, recursively. This is why it must handle circular dependencies — and why it usually cannot.
Lifetimes: transient (new each time), singleton (one per container), scoped (one per request — the one you usually want), container (one per DI container in a modular system).
Wiring by type token: interfaces need a token (the interface type itself, or a symbol/string) since you cannot new an interface.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain difficulty and when you would use it.
Explain the five kinds of injection, and which to use and when you would use it.
Explain an ioc container and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* you stop repeating new chains, you get lifetimes and scoping for free, you can swap bindings per environment. *Cost:* your dependency graph becomes runtime data. Debuggers cannot follow it, stack traces get a resolution frame, mistakes become startup-time "no registration for X" instead of compile-time errors, IDE "go to definition" breaks, and the graph can hide coupling that looks clean in the code. The worst outcome is a codebase where classes have no constructors at all and take everything from a service locator — that is DI without any of its benefits: still hidden dependencies, but now untyped.

topics.title: Circuit breaker, bulkhead, and the resilience pattern family
topics.description: A resilience pattern protects a system from failure in a dependency by failing fast, shedding load, or degrading gracefully, instead of propagating the failure upward.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Circuit breaker
The threshold decision (this is what interviewers ask)
Bulkhead
The rest of the family
Timeout — the single highest-value pattern. Every remote call gets a deadline; the default is "no timeout" which is the worst default.

Retry with exponential backoff + jitter. Jitter is not optional: without it, N clients retry at the same instant after a failure and re-create the overload you were trying to relieve (the *thundering herd*). Use full jitter: sleep = random(0, base * 2^attempt).
Rate limiter (11.4.3) — limit *rate*, breaker limits *failure*.

Fallback / graceful degradation — a cheaper answer when the primary is unavailable (stale cache, default recommendation, "recommendations temporarily unavailable" instead of a 500). Distinguish fallback from circuit-open error: a fallback is a *successful degraded response*.
Load shedding — reject deliberately when overloaded, prioritising important requests. Requires knowing your priority; admission control beats queue collapse.
Hedging — send a duplicate request to a second replica after a delay fraction of the p99; reduces tail latency at the cost of extra load. Use sparingly and only for idempotent reads.
Backpressure — make the queue bounded and reject at the producer. An unbounded queue converts a latency problem into a memory problem and then an outage.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain difficulty and when you would use it.
Explain circuit breaker and when you would use it.
Explain the threshold decision (this is what interviewers ask) and when you would use it.
Explain bulkhead and when you would use it.
Explain the rest of the family and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Every pattern converts *one* failure mode into *another*: latency (queueing), memory (buffering), correctness (stale fallback data), load (retries). The discipline is to have a budget per layer: connect timeout, read timeout, max attempts, total deadline, and make them nested so the inner budget is always smaller than the outer's. A retry budget larger than the caller's deadline is a bug that produces work nobody will read.

topics.title: Saga and the distributed-transaction pattern family
topics.description: A Saga is a sequence of local transactions, each in its own transaction, with compensating actions to undo the logical effects of completed steps when a later step fails. It replaces the 2PC (two-phase commit) database transaction across services.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Why 2PC is not available in microservices
The two flavours, and this is the key question in the interview
Compensation is not rollback. Know these four differences

Compensation cannot undo an observable side effect. email.send() cannot be unsent; you can send an apology. Inventory.decrement() can often be re-incremented but the *history* still shows a decrement, and a warehouse may have physically picked the item. This is the core reason sagas need domain modelling of "semantic rollback".
Compensation may fail, repeatedly. Retry it independently, with its own retry budget, and persist its state so a crash mid-compensation resumes rather than leaks.
Compensation must be idempotent — because it will be retried.

Compensation can be impossible to order. Compensating step 3 without compensating step 2 can leave you worse off (e.g. refunding before cancelling a shipment you then cancel anyway — you end up with a return you did not want). Strict reverse order is the default, and the "already-refunded" checks in compensating actions matter.
Steps: choreography, orchestration, and hybrid
Persistent saga state (this is what makes it production-grade)
Use: when a business transaction spans services and you accept eventual consistency: order + payment + inventory + shipping + notification.
Use: when 2PC is unavailable (different databases, different vendors) or too slow/fragile.

topics.title: Pub/Sub, and how it differs from Observer
topics.description: Publish/Subscribe decouples publishers from subscribers *completely*: the publisher does not know subscribers exist, and subscribers do not know publishers exist. Delivery happens through a broker or mediator. Often asynchronous and cross-process.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The precise difference from Observer
The three questions to answer when choosing

Delivery semantics. at-most-once (ack before handling — you lose data on crash), at-least-once (ack after handling — you get duplicates; this is the only sane default), exactly-once (only within a transaction that includes both the inbox write and the effect — i.e. effectively-once, achieved with the inbox table, not by the broker). State clearly: *exactly-once delivery does not exist; effectively-once processing does, via an idempotent inbox in the same local transaction as the effect.*

Ordering. Brokers guarantee order *per partition*, not globally. If OrderPlaced and OrderShipped must be ordered, both must share a partition key (the order id). Cross-entity ordering requires a different design.

Durability and replay. The event log is durable; consumers track their offset. This gives you replay (rebuild read models — 11.3.7), which is the single most valuable property of event-driven systems and should be your main argument for them.

Schema evolution. Producers and consumers deploy independently. Rules: additive changes only; tolerant reader (ignore unknown fields, require the ones you need); never rename or remove a field; new fields must be optional or have defaults; version in the topic name (orders.placed.v2) with a migration period, or a registry with compatibility checks.
Failure semantics. Poison messages (retries exhausted → DLQ), backpressure (consumer lag), poison-pill prevention, and the fact that a slow consumer in a partition blocks that partition.
Events vs commands on a broker

Use for: cross-service notification, scaling consumers independently, building read models, decoupling release cadence, integrating with external parties, decoupling release cadence, telemetry/audit pipelines, workflow fan-out that must not fail the caller.
Use for "domain event inside one service, 2–4 in-process listeners" — here Observer is better (no broker to run, transactions possible, easier debugging).
Don't use for: anything where the caller needs the result; anything where you cannot tolerate eventual consistency; anything where you cannot operate a broker.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Difficulty:** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Definition.** Publish/Subscribe decouples publishers from subscribers *completely*: the publisher does not know subscribers exist, and subscribers do not know publishers exist. Delivery happens through a broker or mediator. Often asynchronous and cross-process.

**The precise difference from Observer.** The diagram is nearly identical; the *coupling* is not.

| | Observer | Pub/Sub |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subject knows Observers | **Yes** — it holds the list and calls them | **No** — it publishes to a broker |
| Coupling | Compile-time, in-process | Runtime, often cross-service |
| Subscriber knows Subject | Usually yes (it imports the Subject type) | No — it knows only the topic |
| Delivery | Synchronous, same process, in-line | Async (usually), possibly at-least-once |
| Failure of one subscriber | Can affect the others (unless isolated) | Independent, retried by the broker |
| Scaling subscribers | Vertical, one process | Horizontal, add consumers |
| Evolve a subscriber | Requires deploying the Subject's process | Deploy the new subscriber only |
| Failure mode | Bug in your code | Broker down, duplicate delivery, ordering |

**The three questions to answer when choosing.** *Who knows whom? Who is affected by whose failure? Who needs to scale independently?* If subscribers must scale or deploy independently, or if failure isolation matters, you need a broker.

```ts
// ---- Observer: subject holds subscribers. In-process, synchronous.
const bus = new Emitter<Events>();
bus.on('order.placed', p => analytics(p));
bus.emit('order.placed', { id, total });

// ---- Pub/Sub: broker in the middle. Any process, any language, any deploy cadence.
//   Producer: publish to a topic; no subscriber registry exists in this codebase at all.
await broker.publish('orders.placed.v1', { id, total, occurredAt }, {
  key: id,                      // partition key → ordering per entity, not globally
  headers: { 'traceparent': currentTraceparent(), 'tenant': tenantId },
  idempotencyKey: `order.placed:${id}`,
});
//   Consumer: subscribe; may be a service that did not exist when the event was published.
broker.subscribe('orders.placed.v1', async (msg) => {
  const e = parseOrderPlaced(msg);          // (1) parse+validate: unknown fields are fine
  if (await inbox.seen(msg.id)) return;     // (2) idempotency: at-least-once means duplicates
  await projections.upsert(e);              // (3) the actual work, in ONE local transaction with the inbox
  await inbox.mark(msg.id);
}, { concurrency: 8, visibilityTimeoutMs: 30_000 });   // (4) concurrent + ack-after → at-least-once
```

**The five properties you must be able to discuss, because they define the whole design.**

1. **Delivery semantics.** `at-most-once` (ack before handling — you lose data on crash), `at-least-once` (ack after handling — you get duplicates; this is the only sane default), `exactly-once` (only within a transaction that includes both the inbox write and the effect — i.e. **effectively-once**, achieved with the inbox table, not by the broker). State clearly: *exactly-once delivery does not exist; effectively-once processing does, via an idempotent inbox in the same local transaction as the effect.*
2. **Ordering.** Brokers guarantee order *per partition*, not globally. If `OrderPlaced` and `OrderShipped` must be ordered, both must share a partition key (the order id). Cross-entity ordering requires a different design.
3. **Durability and replay.** The event log is durable; consumers track their offset. This gives you replay (rebuild read models — 11.3.7), which is the single most valuable property of event-driven systems and should be your main argument for them.
4. **Schema evolution.** Producers and consumers deploy independently. Rules: additive changes only; tolerant reader (ignore unknown fields, require the ones you need); never rename or remove a field; new fields must be optional or have defaults; version in the topic name (`orders.placed.v2`) with a migration period, or a registry with compatibility checks.
5. **Failure semantics.** Poison messages (retries exhausted → DLQ), backpressure (consumer lag), poison-pill prevention, and the fact that a slow consumer in a partition blocks that partition.

**Events vs commands on a broker.** Name them differently or you will regret it: commands are **imperative and addressed to exactly one logical handler** (`OrderAggregate.reserve.v1`, key = orderId, a handler must exist or it is a bug); events are **declarative facts in the past tense** with **zero or many** handlers (`OrderReserved.v1`, facts that have already happened and cannot be denied). A broker topic named `ProcessPayment` is a command; `PaymentProcessed` is an event. Getting this wrong produces systems where "what happens next" is unknowable because it depends on who is subscribed.

**When to use vs not.**

- **Use** for: cross-service notification, scaling consumers independently, building read models, decoupling release cadence, integrating with external parties, decoupling release cadence, telemetry/audit pipelines, workflow fan-out that must not fail the caller.
- **Use** for "domain event inside one service, 2–4 in-process listeners" — here **Observer is better** (no broker to run, transactions possible, easier debugging).
- **Don't use** for: anything where the caller needs the result; anything where you cannot tolerate eventual consistency; anything where you cannot operate a broker.
- **Don't use** as an excuse to avoid thinking about the flow. **The flow moves; it does not disappear.** Choreographed pub/sub means the sequence of steps lives in *no single place*. That is the whole cost.

**Trade-offs.** *Gain:* independent deployment and scaling, failure isolation, replay, new consumers with no producer change, natural audit trail.
*Cost:* **operational complexity** (a new stateful system to run, back up, secure, and observe), **eventual consistency visible to users**, **harder debugging** (you cannot follow a request; you follow a trace), **schema governance**, **exactly-once illusions**, and **the loss of the ability to read the flow**. Every one of these must be paid before the first benefit arrives.

**Production considerations.**

- **Outbox pattern** for publishing (11.3.6): write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change, then a relay publishes and marks it sent. This eliminates the dual-write problem. If you do nothing else in this section, do this.
- **Consumer idempotency is mandatory**: inbox table + unique constraint on message id, written in the same transaction as the effect.
- **Version every topic**, enforce compatibility in CI with a schema registry or a "tolerant reader" test that deserialises an old fixture with the new code and vice versa.
- **DLQ with alert** and a documented replay procedure (re-drive from DLQ after a fix; ensure handlers are idempotent so replay is safe).
- **Partition key choice is a permanent schema decision** (it determines ordering guarantees). Changing it later means a migration.
- **Consumer lag is the primary SLI** for event-driven systems; alert on it.
- **Correlation/causation ids on every message** (`traceparent`, `causationId`) — without them, distributed tracing across async boundaries is guesswork.
- **Backpressure**: bound consumer concurrency, monitor lag, and shed when lag exceeds a threshold rather than letting every consumer grind.

**Common mistakes.**

1. Publishing events inside the same transaction as the DB write, without an outbox → "committed but never published".
2. Assuming exactly-once → duplicate charges.
3. Renaming a field in a payload → a consumer that was deployed 3 days ago breaks.
4. Publishing events for things that must be ordered, on different keys.
5. Using events for the *primary* flow of a domain that needs immediate answers → confusing, slow, and eventually consistent.
6. No `traceparent` → undebuggable async flows.
7. A topic with 40 subscribers and no owner per subscriber, so nobody knows who may safely change the schema.

**Interviewer probes.**
- *"Observer vs pub/sub — when do you actually need the broker?"* — when subscribers scale/deploy independently or you need failure isolation, replay, or a read model.
- *"How do you guarantee exactly-once?"* — you don't; you get effectively-once via an inbox in the same transaction. The broker's exactly-once claims do not cover your side effects.
- *"What happens if a subscriber is down for an hour?"* — lag grows, then it catches up; capacity must handle catch-up; alert on lag, not on subscriber count.
- *"Why not just call the other service?"* — because that couples availability and deployment. Say which one you would choose here and why.

**Difficulty:** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Definition.** Publish/Subscribe decouples publishers from subscribers *completely*: the publisher does not know subscribers exist, and subscribers do not know publishers exist. Delivery happens through a broker or mediator. Often asynchronous and cross-process.

**The precise difference from Observer.** The diagram is nearly identical; the *coupling* is not.

| | Observer | Pub/Sub |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subject knows Observers | **Yes** — it holds the list and calls them | **No** — it publishes to a broker |
| Coupling | Compile-time, in-process | Runtime, often cross-service |
| Subscriber knows Subject | Usually yes (it imports the Subject type) | No — it knows only the topic |
| Delivery | Synchronous, same process, in-line | Async (usually), possibly at-least-once |
| Failure of one subscriber | Can affect the others (unless isolated) | Independent, retried by the broker |
| Scaling subscribers | Vertical, one process | Horizontal, add consumers |
| Evolve a subscriber | Requires deploying the Subject's process | Deploy the new subscriber only |
| Failure mode | Bug in your code | Broker down, duplicate delivery, ordering |

**The three questions to answer when choosing.** *Who knows whom? Who is affected by whose failure? Who needs to scale independently?* If subscribers must scale or deploy independently, or if failure isolation matters, you need a broker.

```ts
// ---- Observer: subject holds subscribers. In-process, synchronous.
const bus = new Emitter<Events>();
bus.on('order.placed', p => analytics(p));
bus.emit('order.placed', { id, total });

// ---- Pub/Sub: broker in the middle. Any process, any language, any deploy cadence.
//   Producer: publish to a topic; no subscriber registry exists in this codebase at all.
await broker.publish('orders.placed.v1', { id, total, occurredAt }, {
  key: id,                      // partition key → ordering per entity, not globally
  headers: { 'traceparent': currentTraceparent(), 'tenant': tenantId },
  idempotencyKey: `order.placed:${id}`,
});
//   Consumer: subscribe; may be a service that did not exist when the event was published.
broker.subscribe('orders.placed.v1', async (msg) => {
  const e = parseOrderPlaced(msg);          // (1) parse+validate: unknown fields are fine
  if (await inbox.seen(msg.id)) return;     // (2) idempotency: at-least-once means duplicates
  await projections.upsert(e);              // (3) the actual work, in ONE local transaction with the inbox
  await inbox.mark(msg.id);
}, { concurrency: 8, visibilityTimeoutMs: 30_000 });   // (4) concurrent + ack-after → at-least-once
```

**The five properties you must be able to discuss, because they define the whole design.**

1. **Delivery semantics.** `at-most-once` (ack before handling — you lose data on crash), `at-least-once` (ack after handling — you get duplicates; this is the only sane default), `exactly-once` (only within a transaction that includes both the inbox write and the effect — i.e. **effectively-once**, achieved with the inbox table, not by the broker). State clearly: *exactly-once delivery does not exist; effectively-once processing does, via an idempotent inbox in the same local transaction as the effect.*
2. **Ordering.** Brokers guarantee order *per partition*, not globally. If `OrderPlaced` and `OrderShipped` must be ordered, both must share a partition key (the order id). Cross-entity ordering requires a different design.
3. **Durability and replay.** The event log is durable; consumers track their offset. This gives you replay (rebuild read models — 11.3.7), which is the single most valuable property of event-driven systems and should be your main argument for them.
4. **Schema evolution.** Producers and consumers deploy independently. Rules: additive changes only; tolerant reader (ignore unknown fields, require the ones you need); never rename or remove a field; new fields must be optional or have defaults; version in the topic name (`orders.placed.v2`) with a migration period, or a registry with compatibility checks.
5. **Failure semantics.** Poison messages (retries exhausted → DLQ), backpressure (consumer lag), poison-pill prevention, and the fact that a slow consumer in a partition blocks that partition.

**Events vs commands on a broker.** Name them differently or you will regret it: commands are **imperative and addressed to exactly one logical handler** (`OrderAggregate.reserve.v1`, key = orderId, a handler must exist or it is a bug); events are **declarative facts in the past tense** with **zero or many** handlers (`OrderReserved.v1`, facts that have already happened and cannot be denied). A broker topic named `ProcessPayment` is a command; `PaymentProcessed` is an event. Getting this wrong produces systems where "what happens next" is unknowable because it depends on who is subscribed.

**When to use vs not.**

- **Use** for: cross-service notification, scaling consumers independently, building read models, decoupling release cadence, integrating with external parties, decoupling release cadence, telemetry/audit pipelines, workflow fan-out that must not fail the caller.
- **Use** for "domain event inside one service, 2–4 in-process listeners" — here **Observer is better** (no broker to run, transactions possible, easier debugging).
- **Don't use** for: anything where the caller needs the result; anything where you cannot tolerate eventual consistency; anything where you cannot operate a broker.
- **Don't use** as an excuse to avoid thinking about the flow. **The flow moves; it does not disappear.** Choreographed pub/sub means the sequence of steps lives in *no single place*. That is the whole cost.

**Trade-offs.** *Gain:* independent deployment and scaling, failure isolation, replay, new consumers with no producer change, natural audit trail.
*Cost:* **operational complexity** (a new stateful system to run, back up, secure, and observe), **eventual consistency visible to users**, **harder debugging** (you cannot follow a request; you follow a trace), **schema governance**, **exactly-once illusions**, and **the loss of the ability to read the flow**. Every one of these must be paid before the first benefit arrives.

**Production considerations.**

- **Outbox pattern** for publishing (11.3.6): write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change, then a relay publishes and marks it sent. This eliminates the dual-write problem. If you do nothing else in this section, do this.
- **Consumer idempotency is mandatory**: inbox table + unique constraint on message id, written in the same transaction as the effect.
- **Version every topic**, enforce compatibility in CI with a schema registry or a "tolerant reader" test that deserialises an old fixture with the new code and vice versa.
- **DLQ with alert** and a documented replay procedure (re-drive from DLQ after a fix; ensure handlers are idempotent so replay is safe).
- **Partition key choice is a permanent schema decision** (it determines ordering guarantees). Changing it later means a migration.
- **Consumer lag is the primary SLI** for event-driven systems; alert on it.
- **Correlation/causation ids on every message** (`traceparent`, `causationId`) — without them, distributed tracing across async boundaries is guesswork.
- **Backpressure**: bound consumer concurrency, monitor lag, and shed when lag exceeds a threshold rather than letting every consumer grind.

**Common mistakes.**

1. Publishing events inside the same transaction as the DB write, without an outbox → "committed but never published".
2. Assuming exactly-once → duplicate charges.
3. Renaming a field in a payload → a consumer that was deployed 3 days ago breaks.
4. Publishing events for things that must be ordered, on different keys.
5. Using events for the *primary* flow of a domain that needs immediate answers → confusing, slow, and eventually consistent.
6. No `traceparent` → undebuggable async flows.
7. A topic with 40 subscribers and no owner per subscriber, so nobody knows who may safely change the schema.

**Interviewer probes.**
- *"Observer vs pub/sub — when do you actually need the broker?"* — when subscribers scale/deploy independently or you need failure isolation, replay, or a read model.
- *"How do you guarantee exactly-once?"* — you don't; you get effectively-once via an inbox in the same transaction. The broker's exactly-once claims do not cover your side effects.
- *"What happens if a subscriber is down for an hour?"* — lag grows, then it catches up; capacity must handle catch-up; alert on lag, not on subscriber count.
- *"Why not just call the other service?"* — because that couples availability and deployment. Say which one you would choose here and why.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Difficulty:** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Definition.** A pattern anti-pattern is the application of a named pattern in a context where its costs exceed its benefits — producing code that is more abstract, less readable, and no more correct than what it replaced.

**The master heuristic: patterns trade *local* simplicity for *global* flexibility.** You pay locally (one more file, one more indirection) and hope to win globally (change one place when variability arrives). Three questions decide whether the trade paid:

1. **Has the variability actually arrived?** Not "might". Has it arrived twice already?
2. **Is the number of participants small enough that a reader can hold it?** More than ~5 participants in a diagram and you have lost more than you gained.
3. **Is the pattern's cost concentrated where it hurts most?** Indirection in a hot loop or in a CRUD endpoint hurts; indirection in a rarely-changed extension point does not.

**Anti-pattern catalogue, one per pattern, with the smell and the fix.**

| Pattern | How it goes wrong | The smell you will see | The fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Singleton** | Global state + hidden dependency | `X.getInstance()` inside a method; `static reset()` in tests | Inject it; ask for a `Container` singleton lifetime instead |
| **Factory Method / Abstract Factory** | Factory that forwards to a `switch` | `switch (type) { … default: return new … }` inside the factory | Use a registry `Record<Kind, ctor>`; or admit it is a switch and delete the factory |
| **Builder** | Builder that can build anything, including nothing | All-optional fields; no `build()` validation | Required fields in the builder's constructor; or an options object |
| **Adapter** | Adapter containing business rules | `if (customer.isPremium)` inside the adapter | Business rules in a domain service; adapter is translation only |
| **Facade** | Facade as God object | 80 methods, mixed read/write, everyone adds to it | Split by client use case; introduce an application service |
| **Bridge** | Bridge for a single implementation | Interface with exactly one implementor, comment "for future" | Delete it; use the concrete class |
| **Decorator** | Decorator forgetting to forward a method | `undefined is not a function` after someone adds a method | `implements` the interface; a forwarding test |
| **Proxy** | Proxy on a hot path / used as security | Every property access logged in prod; `Proxy` around request objects | Use plain code; use a Proxy only for data-driven rules at the boundary |
| **Observer** | God emitter with 200 event names, no types | Stringly-typed `emit('order.placed')` with no payload type | Typed event map; split the emitter; move cross-process to pub/sub |
| **Command** | One class per trivial method, no undo/queue | `AddTwoCommand` with an `execute()` | Use a function; use Command when it buys deferral/undo/serialisation |
| **Strategy** | Strategy selected by a switch inside the factory | Same problem as the factory anti-pattern | Registry from config; or data table if the branches are data |
| **State** | States that return nothing / no next state | `state.handle()` with `void` returns | It is a Strategy — rename it or make it return the next state |
| **Template Method** | Hook explosion; subclasses that lie | `protected validate() { return true; }` to skip a step | Compose the pipeline; inject steps |
| **Repository** | Generic `BaseRepository<T>` mirroring the ORM | `repo.qb()` in a service; `Repo<any>` | Per-aggregate repos with domain-named methods |
| **Unit of Work** | UoW spanning the whole HTTP request including remote calls | Locks held for seconds | Narrow the transaction; never include a third-party call |
| **DI container** | Service locator; no constructors; unresolvable graph | `Container.get(X)` in a method; circular deps | Composition root + constructor injection |
| **Circuit breaker** | Breaker counting 4xx; global breaker | One breaker per app | Per dependency; count only dependency-health errors |
| **Saga** | Choreography with copied flow logic in every service | Adding a step touches 5 services | Orchestrate the correctness-critical flow |
| **Pub/Sub** | Events for the primary domain flow | `await publish('ProcessPayment')` | Synchronous call for the flow; events for reactions |

**The two most important anti-patterns in practice.**

1. **The Pattern Tax.** When a team learns patterns, they start converting *every* `if` into a class. The measurable outcome: 400 files instead of 60, a new hire takes 3 weeks to understand the checkout flow, and the "flexibility" is never used. The fix is a written rule: *a new file requires a named axis of variation.* Reviewers enforce it. This single rule prevents more damage than any pattern advice.

2. **Diagrammatic Design.** Choosing a pattern because the UML diagram looks impressive, not because a stated requirement varies. The tell: nobody can name the requirement that would justify the indirection. The fix in an interview is to be asked "which requirement drove this?" — if you cannot answer, revert.

**How to review someone else's patterns.** A five-question checklist that works in a real code review:

1. **Point to the requirement that makes this abstract.** If there is none, it should be concrete.
2. **Count the participants.** Over ~5 in one collaboration, the reader's working memory is now the bottleneck.
3. **Find the decision.** Where does the choice of implementation live? If it is a `switch`, the abstraction is decorative.
4. **Delete test.** Remove the pattern, restore the inline code, and diff. If the diff is smaller than the pattern, the pattern loses.
5. **Trace one real request end to end.** If you cannot narrate the flow through the pattern layers without opening 8 files, the indirection is exceeding the abstraction.

**How to talk about this in an interview without sounding anti-pattern.** The winning posture is *eclectic and reasoned*: "I use X when Y, and I deliberately keep Z concrete because …". Anyone can list patterns; the value is in the conditions. The worst answer is "I avoid patterns because they are over-engineering" (you have not thought about the value) or "I use all the GoF patterns" (you have not thought at all).

**Common mistakes.**
- Treating "pattern anti-pattern" as licence to write unstructured code.
- Removing a pattern from a codebase that genuinely varies, to look minimal.
- Reviewing patterns by name rather than by requirement.

**Interviewer probes.**
- *"Which pattern did you remove?"* — the best answer to this question in the entire interview.
- *"How do you decide when a switch is fine?"* — when the branches are few, short, and stable, and when the decision point is the only place that should know about the options.
- *"Our team has 400 files in the payment service. Is that bad?"* — not inherently; it depends on whether the variability is real and whether one person can still narrate the main flow.

Encapsulation
*Data encapsulation*: keeping representation private so it can change freely. The mechanism is access control plus the discipline not to expose mutable internals.

topics.description: A module should have one reason to change — one *axis* of change. Not "does one thing" (vague); "if this reason changes, only this file changes". Software entities are open for extension, closed for modification. In practice: modules you should not need to edit are extended by adding code, not changing code. If S can be used where T is expected, S must be usable *without the caller knowing*. Subtypes must honour the base contract: preconditions cannot be strengthened, postconditions cannot be weakened, and no new exceptions. No client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use. Prefer several small, client-specific interfaces over one fat one. High-level modules must not depend on low-level modules; both must depend on abstractions. Abstractions must not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The practical test
Cross-principle synthesis (this is the part that scores)

Interface-per-class can explode into 20 files with 3-line interfaces; a codebase of pure abstractions is unreadable. Rule of thumb: an abstraction must either have ≥2 implementations (real or planned with a date) or shield a volatile dependency.
Framework magic and DIP fight: Spring, Jackson, and Hibernate want to instantiate and mutate your classes. Accept DI on the framework edge, keep the domain pure.
"Open for extension" without a closing mechanism is a lie — a registry that only one module can write to is not OCP; it is a switch with indirection.
ISP misapplied to create a 1-method interface per method (chatty interfaces: ReadOrderId, ReadOrderTotal). Merge by role, not by method.
DIP applied to your own value objects (IOrder) — absurd.
SRP applied at the-method level until every class is one method.
Liskov violation via "convenience" extra methods that only work on the subtype.
OCP via a giant registry file that everyone edits — which is the switch with extra steps.

*"Which SOLID principle is most violated in practice, and what does it cost?"* — LSP, via base classes that subclasses "specialise" by adding required behaviour; cost: every catch block and every caller is wrong for one subtype.

The DRY failure modes you must know

Premature abstraction. You DRY two things that will diverge. Now you have a function with a boolean flag and a name like doThing(item, isSpecial). The flag is a hidden if, and you have made the code worse while claiming to improve it.

keyConcepts: Difficulty
Why naming is architecture
The eight rules that matter, with the smell each one prevents

```ts
const list = [];          // list of what?
const flag = true;        // flag for what?
// GOOD

const pendingSettlements: Settlement[] = [];
const isRetryEligible: boolean = /* … */;
```

2. **Booleans read as predicates, and positive names are safer.** `isActive`, `hasCapacity`, `shouldRetry`, `canRefund`. Avoid double negatives (`isNotDisabled`) and avoid names that invite the wrong call: `deleteQuietly` (does it delete?), `close()` (does it free resources?).

5. **Collections are plural, singular is one item.** `order`, `orders`, `orderIds`. Distinguish `user` (the entity) from `userId` (the reference) from `userRepository`. The `Id` suffix is non-negotiable in TypeScript.

7. **`get` means retrieval; `find` means retrieval that can fail to find; `load` means retrieval that does I/O; `create` means construction that may or may not persist.** These conventions are worth having because they answer "can this return null?" at the call site without reading the body:

```ts

getUser(id: string): Promise<User>              // throws NotFound if absent

requireUser(id): User                           // sync, throws
```

- **Prefix with the mechanism when the distinction matters**: `parseOrderRow` vs `loadOrderRow` vs `fetchOrderRow`.

- **Version in the name only for external contracts** (`OrdersApiV2`), never for internal code.
- **Negations**: `!isEligible` is fine in a private boolean; `noRetry` in a public config is a bug factory — use `retry: boolean`.
- **Avoid an `Impl` suffix** except to distinguish an interface from its only production implementation in a codebase with genuine plugin variance; `InMemoryUserRepository` says more than `UserRepositoryImpl`.

Fix by finding the noun it actually manages and the verb it actually performs.

1. Abbreviations: `ordSvc`, `calcAmt`, `qty` (fine in an invoice line, not in an order API), `proc`.

3. `get2`, `newOrder`, `orderNew` — versioned-by-append names indicate unclear ownership.
4. Inconsistent synonyms for one concept across the codebase.

- Naming discipline erodes under deadline pressure; put a lint rule or a review checklist item in, otherwise it depends on memory.

- *"What's the most common naming mistake you see?"* — `get` that may return null, and `handler`/`manager` nouns that mean nothing.
- *"How do you handle naming collisions between the domain and the API?"* — deliberate suffix scheme: domain `Order`, DTO `OrderView`, command `PlaceOrder`; never reuse one name for two shapes.

topics.title: Anemic domain models and when they are fine
topics.description: An anemic domain model consists of data-carrying classes with getters/setters and all behaviour in a separate service layer. It is the default outcome of naive layering, and it is the most common criticism of "clean architecture".
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The four costs of anemic models, stated precisely
Invalid states are representable. Any combination of fields is assignable. The compiler will not stop you, so the check happens in some service you forgot about.
Invariant duplication and drift. The same rule appears in every service that touches the entity; one of them will be out of date.
"Transaction script" sprawl. Services become scripts that do many things each, and each service can be entered from a different starting state.
The model cannot be reused. The next use case (a CLI, a scheduled job, a webhook) re-implements the rules differently, and now the rules exist four times.
An anemic model is the right choice when
The entity is mostly data with almost no invariants. A UserProfile, an AuditLogEntry, a Product in a catalogue: behaviour is CRUD and any "logic" is a projection. A rich model here is ceremony.
The logic is fundamentally about coordination, not about a single entity's invariants: an ETL job, an import/export pipeline, an API gateway, an orchestrator.
The domain is CRUD and the interesting complexity is in the UI or the queries. Content management, an admin panel, a simple catalogue.
The data is shared and write-heavy from many angles, and the "rules" are actually access rules → then your rules belong in the schema (constraints, permissions) and a service, not in a domain class.
You are serving a machine consumer, not a human. Anemic DTOs + a validation library is exactly right.
